clips.start_words: One of the ingredients that are in food
clips.send: Someone who packs school lunches sends this to the other parent on sandwich duty: the actual ingredient, and why it's legal - the quiet alarm of finding out what's really in the bread you hand your kid every morning.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau on an ingredient most people have never heard of, in bread most people eat every week.

It's called azodicarbonamide. It's also used to make yoga mats and shoe soles. As a dough conditioner, it's added to bread to make it spongier and keep it from crumbling, and studies have linked it to asthma and other health problems.

The FDA calls it toxic but allows it in small amounts. One report once found it in close to 500 foods, including a 100% whole wheat loaf.

Does your bread's label mention a dough conditioner?

clips.send: Someone who just noticed their bread never goes stale sends this to whoever buys the groceries: the two-day test that tells you something's off - the unease of realizing your fresh bread might not be food at all.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau's simple test for the bread in your kitchen.

His claim: real bread, the kind made in Italy or France and bought fresh each morning, gets hard within a day. No conditioners, nothing to stop it. If a loaf in your pantry sits soft for days without turning hard as a rock or moldy, he says that's the tell - something in there is keeping it soft that isn't on the label.

His point isn't about one brand. It's about the whole shelf.

Go press on your bread today. Hard yet, or still soft?
